name: Agile Project Management
objectives: Given a project description, explain how Agile runs the work in short rounds and when waterfall fits better, in your own words, with one example of each
Given a small Scrum team, name the three Scrum accountabilities, the five events and the three artifacts, getting at least 9 of 11 right
For a real project of two to six weeks, write a backlog of at least eight user stories with acceptance criteria, in priority order, with every story in the "As a..., I want... so that..." pattern
Given your backlog and the hours you really have, plan a one-week sprint with a one-sentence sprint goal and tasks of a day or less, so the planned work fits the time you have
During your sprint, track the work on a task board with a WIP limit and a daily 15-minute check-in, moving every card as the work happens
At the end of your sprint, hold a sprint review and a Keep, Stop, Try retrospective and add one improvement to the next sprint, with feedback written into the backlog

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Agile is, and how it differs from a big plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words how Agile runs a project in short rounds.
This lesson builds toward: Given a project description, you will explain how Agile runs the work in short rounds and when waterfall fits better, in your own words, with one example of each.
In a traditional or "waterfall" project, you plan everything up front, then build it, then test it, then deliver it at the end. That works when the job is well known, like pouring a foundation. It breaks down when needs change halfway through.
Agile delivers in short rounds, often one to four weeks. Each round produces something usable, the team shows it to the people it is for, and the plan is adjusted based on what they say. The Agile Manifesto (2001) puts it simply: working results and responding to change matter more than following a fixed plan.
Scrum and Kanban are the two most common ways to do Agile. Scrum uses fixed-length rounds called sprints. Kanban uses a board and a steady flow of work with a limit on how much is in progress at once. You can use ideas from both.
Words to know:
- Agile: a way of running projects in short rounds, with frequent checks and changes.
- Waterfall: a way of running projects where each phase is finished before the next begins.
- Scrum: an Agile method that works in fixed-length rounds called sprints.
- Kanban: an Agile method that uses a board and limits how much work is in progress.
Official sources:
- Manifesto for Agile Software Development
- The Scrum Guide (2020)
Try it now: Choose one real project you want to finish in the next two to six weeks. Write one sentence describing it and one sentence about who it is for.
You can now explain how Agile differs from a big up-front plan and name Scrum and Kanban.

options: A way of doing Agile with a board and a limit on work in progress
check.why: Kanban uses a board and a steady flow of work with a limit on how much is in progress.

check.q: Your veterans' group is building a new website, and members keep changing what they want. Which approach fits?
options: Waterfall: plan it all up front and deliver at the end
Agile: deliver in short rounds and adjust after each one
Wait until everyone agrees on everything
check.why: Agile suits work where needs change, because each round is shown and the plan is adjusted.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scrum roles, events and artifacts
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name who does what in Scrum and the five events a sprint uses.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small Scrum team, you will name the three Scrum accountabilities, the five events and the three artifacts, getting at least 9 of 11 right.
The Scrum Guide (2020 version) names three accountabilities. The Product Owner decides what matters most and keeps the list of work in order. The Developers are the people doing the work, of any kind, not only software. The Scrum Master helps the team follow Scrum and removes blockers.
There are five events. The Sprint is the container, one month or less. Sprint Planning sets the sprint goal and picks the work. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute check on progress toward the goal. The Sprint Review shows the results to the people the work is for. The Sprint Retrospective looks at how the team worked and picks improvements.
There are three artifacts: the Product Backlog (all the work, in order), the Sprint Backlog (the work chosen for this sprint) and the Increment (the usable result). On a small project, one person may hold more than one role. That is fine as long as each job gets done.
Words to know:
- Product Owner: the person who decides what work matters most and orders the backlog.
- Scrum Master: the person who helps the team use Scrum well and clears blockers.
- Increment: the usable result a sprint produces.
- Retrospective: a meeting at the end of a sprint about how the team worked; similar to an after-action review.
Official sources:
- The Scrum Guide (2020)
Try it now: For your project, write who will act as Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers. If it is just you, write which hat you will wear at each event.
You can now name the three Scrum accountabilities, the five events and the three artifacts, and assign them on your project.

check.q: What is the Increment in Scrum?
options: The usable result produced by the sprint
The list of all the work
check.why: The Increment is the usable result; the Product Backlog is the list of all work.

check.q: You are the only person on a small project. What do you do about the Scrum roles?
options: Stop, because Scrum needs at least three people
Hold more than one role and make sure each job gets done
check.why: On a small project one person may hold more than one role, as long as each job gets done.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing user stories and building a backlog
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn a project into a prioritized backlog of user stories with clear finish lines.
This lesson builds toward: For a real project of two to six weeks, you will write a backlog of at least eight user stories with acceptance criteria, in priority order, with every story in the "As a..., I want... so that..." pattern.
A user story describes a piece of work from the point of view of the person it helps: "As a [type of person], I want [something] so that [reason]." For example: "As a hiring manager, I want a one-page résumé so that I can see the candidate's skills fast."
Each story needs acceptance criteria: two or three checks that say when it is done. For the résumé story: fits on one page, lists three measurable results, has no spelling errors. Clear finish lines stop arguments later.
Put the stories in order: most valuable and most urgent at the top. An AI assistant like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can help you draft stories from a project description, but you decide the order and check that each story is real work.
Step by step:
- List everything the project needs, one item per line.
- Rewrite each item as "As a..., I want... so that...".
- Add two or three acceptance criteria to each.
- Split any story too big to finish in one sprint.
- Put the stories in priority order, top to bottom.
Words to know:
- User story: a short description of work from the point of view of the person it helps.
- Acceptance criteria: the checks that say a story is done.
- Backlog: the ordered list of all work for the project.
Try it now: Write at least eight user stories for your project, each with acceptance criteria, and put them in priority order. You may ask an AI assistant: "Turn this project into user stories with acceptance criteria" and then edit the result.
You can now write user stories with acceptance criteria and order them into a backlog.

check.q: What does the "so that" part of a user story give?
check.why: "So that" states the reason or benefit for the person the story helps.

check.q: An AI assistant drafts stories for your community event. One is "Plan the whole event". What do you do?
options: Split it into smaller stories that fit in one sprint
Keep it as the top story
check.why: A story too big for one sprint should be split into smaller pieces.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Planning a sprint with a clear goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a one- or two-week sprint with a sprint goal and the right amount of work.
This lesson builds toward: Given your backlog and the hours you really have, you will plan a one-week sprint with a one-sentence sprint goal and tasks of a day or less, so the planned work fits the time you have.
Sprint Planning answers three questions: why is this sprint valuable (the sprint goal), what can be done (which stories), and how will it be done (the tasks).
A sprint goal is one sentence, like a commander's intent: "By Friday, I have a finished résumé and five tailored applications sent." If plans change midway, the goal tells everyone what still matters.
Take stories from the top of the backlog until the team's time is full, and leave some slack. New teams almost always plan too much. Break each story into tasks of a day or less.
Step by step:
- Decide the sprint length (one or two weeks is good for beginners).
- Write a one-sentence sprint goal.
- Pull stories from the top of the backlog that serve the goal.
- Break each story into tasks of a day or less.
- Check the total against the hours you really have, and cut if needed.
Words to know:
- Sprint goal: one sentence saying what the sprint is meant to achieve.
- Capacity: how much time the team really has during the sprint.
Try it now: Plan a one-week sprint for your project: write the sprint goal, pick the stories, break them into tasks, and check them against the hours you actually have this week.
You can now plan a sprint with a goal, chosen stories and tasks that fit your real time.

check.q: How long should a task in a sprint plan ideally take?
check.why: Breaking stories into tasks of a day or less makes progress easy to track.

check.q: Halfway through the sprint, plans change. What tells the team what still matters?
options: The oldest card on the board
check.why: Like commander's intent, the sprint goal says what still matters when plans change.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running the work on a task board
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a task board and use a daily check-in to keep work moving.
This lesson builds toward: During your sprint, you will track the work on a task board with a WIP limit and a daily 15-minute check-in, moving every card as the work happens.
A task board shows the work in columns: To Do, In Progress and Done. Each task is a card that moves right as work happens. You can use sticky notes on a wall, a spreadsheet, or a free board tool such as Trello, Microsoft Planner or GitHub Projects.
Kanban adds a work-in-progress (WIP) limit: for example, no more than two cards In Progress per person. Finishing work beats starting new work.
The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes. Each person shares progress toward the sprint goal, what is next, and anything blocking them. Blockers get solved after the meeting, not during it.
Step by step:
- Make three columns: To Do, In Progress, Done.
- Add one card per task from your sprint plan.
- Set a WIP limit, such as two cards In Progress.
- Each day, move cards and hold a 15-minute check-in.
- Write down blockers and who will clear them.
Words to know:
- Task board: a board with columns showing where each task stands.
- WIP limit: a cap on how many tasks can be in progress at once.
- Blocker: anything stopping a task from moving forward.
Try it now: Build a task board for your sprint with three columns and one card per task. Set a WIP limit. For the next three days, move the cards and write a two-line daily check-in.
You can now run a sprint on a task board with a WIP limit and a short daily check-in.

check.q: What three things does each person share at the Daily Scrum?
options: Their opinion of the Product Owner
Progress toward the goal, what is next and any blockers
check.why: The Daily Scrum is a short check on progress toward the sprint goal, next steps and blockers.

check.q: You finish a task. What do you do with its card?
options: Throw it away before anyone sees it
Move it back to To Do
check.why: Cards move right as work happens, so a finished task goes to Done.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Closing the sprint: review and retrospective
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Hold a sprint review and a retrospective and turn them into one change for the next sprint.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of your sprint, you will hold a sprint review and a Keep, Stop, Try retrospective and add one improvement to the next sprint, with feedback written into the backlog.
The Sprint Review shows the finished work to the people it is for and asks what they think. Only show work that meets its acceptance criteria. Their feedback goes back into the backlog.
The Sprint Retrospective is about how you worked, not what you built. It works like an after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to do differently. A simple format is Keep, Stop, Try.
Pick one improvement and put it into the next sprint as a real task. A retrospective that changes nothing is just a meeting. Agile certifications, such as the Certified ScrumMaster from Scrum Alliance or the Professional Scrum Master from Scrum.org, can come later; check their sites for current requirements and fees.
Step by step:
- List what was finished and meets its acceptance criteria.
- Show it to the people it is for and write down their feedback.
- Add the feedback to the backlog.
- Hold a Keep / Stop / Try retrospective.
- Put one improvement into the next sprint.
Words to know:
- Sprint Review: a meeting to show finished work and get feedback.
- After-action review: a military debrief on what was planned, what happened and what to change.
- Keep / Stop / Try: a simple retrospective format.
Official sources:
- Scrum Alliance: Certified ScrumMaster
- Scrum.org assessments
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-week sprint. Write a short sprint review (what is done, who saw it, what they said) and a Keep / Stop / Try retrospective, then add one improvement to the next sprint.
You can now close a sprint with a review and a retrospective and carry one improvement into the next sprint.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Backlog of user stories Fewer than eight stories, or items written as plain tasks with no "so that". At least eight stories in the pattern, each with two or three acceptance criteria, in priority order. Big stories are split and the learner can explain why the top story is first. Sprint plan No sprint goal, or the work is more than the time available. A one-sentence sprint goal, stories from the top of the backlog and tasks of a day or less that fit the hours. Leaves some slack and says what would be cut first. Task board The board was set up but cards were not moved during the week. To Do, In Progress and Done columns, a WIP limit and cards moved daily. Blockers were written down with who cleared them. Review and retrospective The review or the retrospective is missing. A written review with feedback added to the backlog, and Keep, Stop and Try listed. One improvement is already a task in the next sprint. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A retrospective is most like which military practice?
check.why: Like an after-action review, it asks what was planned, what happened, why, and what to change.

check.q: Your team listed five things to try next sprint. What makes the retrospective count?
options: Write them down and forget them
Pick one and add it to the next sprint as a real task
Hold another meeting to discuss them
check.why: One improvement turned into a real task is what changes how the team works.
